stories.headline: Does the law back Enes Kanter Freedom's WNBA draft bid?
stories.summary: Enes Kanter Freedom declared himself a woman and said he's eligible for the WNBA draft. Legal experts point out strengths and flaws in his case.
stories.body:
The WNBA returned to action Thursday night after a three-week break. Congress welcomed the league back by demanding answers about eligibility and accountability.

In a Sept. 17 letter addressed to WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert, five members of the U.S. House of Representatives, including a representative from Indiana, criticized the league for not prioritizing player and fan safety. Among the concerns was how the WNBA determines who is eligible to play.

"As a women's sports league, the WNBA must ensure the League remains exclusively for biological women," the letter said. "As Sophie Cunningham has commented, women should not have to face biological men playing in the WNBA. Opening eligibility to biological men would not only create an unfair advantage but would also risk player safety for the women playing in the WNBA."

Debate around who is eligible to play in the WNBA has raged since Cunningham told ESPN in a July 21 article that she supported restrictions on transgender girls and women in girls' and women's sports.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" the Fever guard said in the article. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Demonstrations supporting and criticizing Cunningham popped up at Fever games across the country in July and August. Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom stoked the flames by declaring for the WNBA draft in an Instagram post.

"If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," Kanter Freedom said, wearing an orange WNBA hoodie, in the Aug. 7 video.

The 6-foot-10 Kanter Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA and last appeared for the Celtics on Feb. 8, 2022. Hours later, former fringe NBA player Royce White also declared for the draft.

Kanter Freedom sat in a baseline seat for an Aug. 23 game between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever wearing a black shirt that read, "Woman noun. adult human female." After scoring on an acrobatic layup in the third quarter, Natasha Cloud walked toward the baseline and yelled at him. Kanter Freedom stretched out his arms and stepped toward Cloud as she was surrounded by teammates and security.

Kanter Freedom was ejected from the game.

While most people in and around the WNBA don't believe Kanter Freedom and White are acting in good faith, the former NBA players have exposed potential WNBA legal vulnerabilities.

Matt Gaetz, White's attorney, did not respond to an interview request from ESPN. An interview with an attorney from the America First Policy Institute, which represents Kanter Freedom, was scheduled and then canceled by the institute. An institute spokesperson did not respond to repeated attempts to reschedule.

Cunningham and the Fever return to the court Friday night for the first time since Aug. 28, when White sat courtside at Indiana's Gainbridge Fieldhouse wearing a blond wig. What could possibly be next?

ESPN spoke to five employment attorneys as well as league and union sources -- some speaking on the condition of anonymity -- seeking answers.

Who is eligible to play in the WNBA?

The 2026 CBA states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." Similar clauses have been in each of the league's six CBAs beginning with the first in 1999. The document does not elaborate on who the WNBA considers to be a woman or any process by which a transgender woman could become eligible. The WNBA is not alone. The National Women's Soccer League adopted a gender eligibility policy in 2021 but abandoned it in 2022. "Our policies are our practice, which is that every player who plays in this league has been determined to be eligible, and we're continuing to apply that on a consistent basis," NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman told reporters in August. The Professional Women's Hockey League also operates without a formal policy and there is no statement of eligibility in its CBA.

The policy landscape in elite women's sports has shifted significantly in the past half-decade. From 2015-21, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) allowed transgender women to compete in the women's category provided they suppressed their testosterone below a specific threshold for one year. The NCAA operated under a similar policy from 2010-22. Both organizations also had rules for transgender men and intersex athletes. The NCAA has since restricted women's sports in all three divisions to only those whose birth sex is female. The IOC went a step further, barring transgender and intersex women from women's competition. The U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee has pushed similar bans through the national governing bodies.

Is it legal for a business to require its employees to be a specific sex?

Almost never. But sometimes. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars discrimination in employment on the basis of a number of traits, including sex. However, it allows for something called a bona fide occupational qualification. It's defined as a "limited exception for discrimination based on sex, religion, or national origin" if it is a necessary qualification for the business or the job. As an example, opening casting for the title character in "Erin Brockovich" only to women is fine.

So is the WNBA immune to claims of sex-based discrimination?

Not even close. The WNBA, which operates in multiple states, is subject to both state and federal anti-discrimination laws. Title VII states it is unlawful for an employer "to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual ... because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin." In 2020, the Supreme Court ruled in Bostock v. Clayton County, Georgia, that firing someone "merely for being gay or transgender" violated Title VII.

Members of WNBA teams are not just athletes, they are employees. The legality of a transgender athlete policy in American women's professional sports has never been litigated.

The WNBA could enact a policy that would bar anyone whose birth sex was not female from playing in the league. Alternatively, the WNBA could enact a policy that would establish a process by which a transgender or intersex woman could play in the league. If challenged, the league and/or the union would have a path in court to argue the policy should be permissible as a bona fide occupational qualification.

"What the WNBA would argue, I think, if they were presented with this issue, is, you know, the essence of our business is we are a women's sports league, so therefore we can restrict this," said Nathan J. Oleson, an employment lawyer and shareholder at Littler Mendelson. "They can use that sort of defense to argue we only want women who were assigned female at birth, or we want to define women to include transgender females and define where on the spectrum we determine that those people become women."

Does Title IX contain any direction for the league?

The Supreme Court ruled in 2026 that state laws barring transgender women and girls from school and collegiate sports did not violate Title IX. The 1972 law is often invoked as being synonymous with women's sports, but it bars sex-based discrimination in education, including extracurricular programs, funded by schools. Title IX required schools and colleges to fund girls' and women's sports or risk losing federal funding. The WNBA is a private business and not subject to Title IX because it's not an educational institution.

Has a transgender woman ever played in the WNBA?

No. Two nonbinary athletes have played for WNBA teams, but both of those athletes' birth sex was female.

What are the paths for a transgender woman to play in the WNBA, and how hard would it be to make the league?

It's a stretch to think that any up-and-coming American transgender girl or woman would be able to navigate all the obstacles in her way. For one, fewer than half the states allow transgender girls to compete in high school girls' sports. If a transgender girl played in one of the 21 states that still does allow it, then the door would be closed in college because the NCAA has banned transgender women from women's competition in all three divisions. Same for NAIA. It's worth noting that even when transgender girls and women could follow a tried-and-true path, none made it to the WNBA. Take away the coaching and competition benefits in high school and college, and the possibility goes from slim to virtually none.

In theory, a gifted, young trans athlete in the U.S. could find somewhere to play abroad until she's draft-eligible and then be drafted by a WNBA team. There is a 34-year-old transgender woman currently playing in the second-tier French league who could potentially be eligible for the WNBA, but given her age and that she's not a top-level player in the country's best league, she's not likely to get a look by the WNBA, which is considerably more competitive.

A transgender woman transitioning as an adult or after beginning an athletic career in men's sports could also seek entry into the league like Renee Richards did in women's tennis in the 1970s. But that has never happened in the league's 30-year history.

What has the WNBA said about Kanter Freedom and White's eligibility for the 2027 draft?

Following a meeting of the league's anti-hate task force on Aug. 12, the WNBA released a statement, implying that Kanter Freedom and White are not eligible to be drafted. "There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others," the statement read in part. The WNBA declined to clarify to ESPN how it came to that determination.

The 2026 CBA does not contain a clear answer. The CBA lays out the criteria for someone to be draft-eligible, but it focuses on age. A player competing in the United States must be turning 22 years old the year of the draft and have no remaining college eligibility or renounce that eligibility. Players are also eligible if they've graduated from college, or will within three months of the draft and have either exhausted their eligibility or renounced it. The same is true for players who did not attend college, as long as they are four years removed from high school.

International athletes playing abroad either at the amateur or professional levels are eligible if they will be 20 the year of the draft. If an international athlete plays in the NCAA, they are subject to the same criteria as American players playing collegiate basketball in the United States.

Kanter Freedom, who came to the United States from Turkey to play basketball when he was 17, was 20 in 2012. Royce White grew up in Minnesota. He graduated high school in 2009 and was in the 2013 collegiate class.

The CBA says that players are eligible for two WNBA drafts and three for late-matriculating international players. Athletes are eligible to be signed as free agents if they have previously been eligible for the WNBA draft. If White and Kanter Freedom had been eligible for a previous draft -- which seems implausible considering they never identified as women before -- they would now be eligible to be signed.

Can Kanter Freedom and White sue to try and play in the WNBA?

This is where things get interesting. To bring a Title VII claim, Kanter Freedom and White would need to file with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). The EEOC could investigate, and if it finds cause to believe discrimination occurred, the agency could sue the WNBA. The agency can also, however, opt not to investigate itself and issue a "right to sue" notice to the party alleging discrimination, clearing the way for a lawsuit. According to Oleson, a Title VII claim could be dismissed from court and sent to arbitration if there is a "clear and unmistakable" agreement to handle discrimination claims through arbitration in the CBA.

State employment laws also apply. If Kanter Freedom and White were to press the issue of their eligibility by bringing a state-level claim, and the players' union agreed with their position, but the league did not, Oleson says that would likely trigger arbitration under the Labor Management Relations Act (LMRA) to decide how "women" should be defined.

"There's a long line of case authority under federal labor law," Oleson said. "It says because we have such a strong interest in this country in allowing unions and employers to figure out their disputes based on the processes they've agreed to, that if there's a dispute about what 'woman' means under the [WNBA] CBA, that goes to arbitration. It doesn't go straight to the court system."

If, however, the WNBPA and the league both agreed that Kanter Freedom and White were ineligible under the current CBA, LMRA would not apply and a case could proceed to court.

Can teams just quietly agree to not draft or sign Kanter Freedom and White?

If they did, it would violate the CBA. The CBA bars teams from entering "into any contracts, combinations or conspiracies, express or implied, with the WNBA or any other WNBA Team, their employees or agents" to decide who should or should not be offered an opportunity in the WNBA. In other words, the league bars collusion. This is standard practice in professional sports, but there have been accusations of collusion. In the 1980s, for example, the MLBPA accused the owners of colluding to suppress free-agent salaries. The owners paid the union a $280 million settlement in 1990.

Collusion aside, each team could independently decide not to sign Kanter Freedom or White for a variety of reasons. There are players who are good enough to play in the WNBA right now who are not on rosters because of concerns about chemistry, commitment, work ethic or other reasons routinely cited by hiring managers choosing between job candidates. That does not immediately mean WNBA teams colluded to keep them out. Such an allegation would have to be proven, either in court or arbitration.

So what arguments could be made in court?

If Kanter Freedom and White decided to sue to try and force the WNBA to let them play, a relevant legal question would be their identities. When White announced that he would be eligible for the draft, he told Fox News Digital, "I'm transgender. I'm a woman. I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball, professional basketball, so I'll be declaring for the WNBA draft in 2027 as well."

In a lawsuit filed on Sept. 3 arguing the Chicago Sky violated his First Amendment rights when he was ejected from the Aug. 23 Sky game against the Fever, Kanter Freedom is referred to with he/him pronouns and the document says that Kanter Freedom "has self-identified as a player who is eligible to play in the WNBA." It does not identify him as a woman.

In general, the courts take identity at face value. In states that allow transgender girls to compete in girls' sports without legal or medical intervention, like Connecticut, it's not uncommon to require a level of identity authenticity, often proved through school records and how a student presents in school activities. Kanter Freedom and White saying they are transgender would likely be litigated, specifically questioning the authenticity of those claims.

"And then you know what would be discoverable? Any and all text messages, communications, emails, phone calls that they have had about this topic and about this stunt," said Susie Cirilli, an employment law expert at Spector Gadon Rosen Vinci P.C. who represents a number of transgender athletes.

Kanter Freedom and White would be deposed under oath. They could be asked to produce medical and psychological records corroborating their claims of being transgender women. Friends, family and agents could also be deposed.

"It would be my strong expectation that if a person claims to be transgender and alleged a legal claim and the defendant could establish that the plaintiff was not transgender, that would suffice to defeat the claim," said another lawyer, requesting anonymity, who has worked on transgender issues.

Kanter Freedom says he meets "every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," but what about testosterone levels?

There is a robust anti-doping protocol outlined in the CBA. Players are randomly tested at intervals throughout the season for banned substances, including testosterone. There is no publicly available threshold for naturally occurring (endogenous) testosterone in the CBA. The league and union declined to answer questions from ESPN about the process should a player have higher than expected endogenous testosterone.

What policy could the WNBA enact if it did not want to include transgender and intersex women?

The WNBA could choose to enact a policy that defines "woman" as determined by birth sex, specifically requiring an SRY-gene test, which is already being used in some international competitions. An SRY-gene test is a proxy for identifying the presence of a Y chromosome. Transgender women have Y chromosomes because their birth sex is male. However, there are athletes with intersex variations who may also test positive for the SRY-gene.

Andrew Sinclair discovered the SRY-gene in 1990 and has pushed back against its use for this purpose. "Using SRY to establish biological sex is wrong because all it tells you is whether or not the gene is present," Sinclair wrote in The Conversation. "It does not tell you how SRY is functioning, whether a testis has formed, whether testosterone is produced and, if so, whether it can be used by the body."

For some, exclusion is the only legal path forward.

"In most cases, sex doesn't matter for the law, and in fact, taking it into account is what the law is trying to prevent," said Inez Feltscher Stepman, a legal analyst for the Independent Women's Law Center. "But in some cases, the law requires that you recognize sex."

What policy could the WNBA enact if it wanted to include transgender and intersex women?

Prior to 2020 when Idaho passed the first law that barred transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports and kicked off a wave of similar legislative and policy changes, sports leagues and governing bodies allowed transgender women to compete in the women's category under specific conditions. The WNBA could choose to adopt a similar policy that requires testosterone suppression under a threshold for a specific duration.

Similarly, the WNBA could expound upon its definition of "woman" in a way that allows for some intersex women to be eligible.

Any such policy would likely be litigated.

"There's always been requirements to do a job, and so this is just the next thing that lawyers, and people in the league need to put their heads together on," Cirilli said. "But the result cannot be exclusion that violates federal law."

If the WNBA opts to codify its policy, how does that process work?

Eligibility to play in the league is collectively bargained, so any change would likely need to be as well. Following the anti-hate task force's meeting last month, the WNBA said conversations will continue. "We will continue to engage all league stakeholders in the coming weeks and months," the statement read in part. "We will approach these important conversations thoughtfully and in alignment with the values of our league."

A major factor for the WNBA is the commissioner. Engelbert announced on Sept. 4 that she plans to depart her role at the end of 2026. Her replacement will be an important voice in the discussion.

That likely makes any substantive policy change a long way off.

The union, when asked by ESPN, declined to comment on its stance on Kanter Freedom and White's eligibility. Some players, including Cloud, Stefanie Dolson and union executive committee member Brianna Turner, have shown support for transgender inclusion broadly. Most have remained silent. Cunningham, when asked last week by ESPN, did not endorse the NBA players' eligibility claims.

"I'm gonna let them do them," she said.

stories.headline: UFC 331 preview and picks: Pantoja sees opportunity in disaster
stories.summary: Top storylines and coaches' analysis for UFC 331 in Los Angeles.
stories.body:
For two and a half years, Alexandre Pantoja ruled the UFC's flyweight division at a level unseen since the historic era of Demetrious Johnson nearly 10 years ago. And yet, the past nine months since his last fight could prove to be the most compelling of Pantoja's career.
The 36-year-old Pantoja (30-6) will challenge Joshua Van (17-2) for the 125-pound championship at UFC 331 inside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Saturday. It will be his first appearance since UFC 323 in December, when he lost the belt to Van via TKO after Pantoja suffered a dislocated elbow 26 seconds into the fight. The nature of the loss has led to a feeling of unfinished business between the two fighters going into Saturday's main event.

"As an athlete, yes, I have a TKO loss on my record," Pantoja told ESPN. "I've never lost by TKO or submission before. Nobody had ever finished me. Now, I have that. But personally, as a man? No. I don't believe I have a loss to him."

Pantoja won the title against Brandon Moreno in 2023 and defended the belt four times before meeting Van. He was among the best pound-for-pound fighters in the world at the time. But with a comeback narrative attached to him for this fight, he said there is an added level of excitement.

"For sure, this is an opportunity," Pantoja said. "In my soul, that's the opportunity. Now, I get to fight the champion. He's the champion of the world and I love that. It makes the fight more spicy for me."

Van, 24, has embraced the narrative -- even while cementing himself as the undisputed champion. There are those who say Van needs to defeat Pantoja again to legitimize his championship, but Van's first title defense against Tatsuro Taira in May made discrediting him harder. Taira's ground game posed a real threat to Van, but he ultimately knocked out the Japanese challenger in the fifth round of a matchup that earned fight of the night honors at UFC 328.

The unfinished business, Pantoja's return and Van's undeniable star power mean Saturday's flyweight title fight is shaping up to be the most anticipated 125-pound title fight since Henry Cejudo ended Johnson's nearly five-year title reign in 2018 then defended the flyweight belt against then-bantamweight champion TJ Dillashaw in 2019.

For Pantoja specifically, his worst stroke of bad luck could turn into the greatest night of his career.

"Saturday night is going to be my best night, man," Pantoja said. "I haven't been to work in 10 months. That's why all of these fights, and this one especially, is worth so much. We work for months to just get one night of work. I've recovered my arm. Now I have an opportunity to show everyone what I did in the last 10 months."

More storylines to watch
History isn't in Pantoja's favor
If Alexandre Pantoja is searching for role models to inspire this weekend's quest to reclaim the championship he lost suddenly and painfully last December, he would be wise to look beyond recent history.

Within the past two weeks, two of the UFC's 11 champs -- women's flyweight Valentina Shevchenko and heavyweight Tom Aspinall -- vacated their titles because of health issues. Their paths back to the top of the mountain are as yet uncharted.

Before them, the most recent champions to lose their titles to injuries did not fare well upon their returns. In November 2022, Jiří Procházka vacated the UFC light heavyweight title after hurting his shoulder in training. His successor was Jamahal Hill, who just months after winning the vacant title had to vacate it himself after rupturing an Achilles. As soon as he was healed, Hill was granted an opportunity to reclaim his title and lost. Procházka was given three shots at the 205-pound belt and fell short in all of them.

For a success story, Pantoja must look deeper into UFC championship history to the brutal health issues overcome by Dominick Cruz. While preparing for a bantamweight title defense in May 2012, Cruz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee. He underwent surgery, then had a setback requiring a second ACL surgery six months later. He was scheduled to return in February 2014 but suffered a groin tear in training. Facing another extended recovery, he vacated his title.

Cruz returned that September and won a fight that put him in position for a shot at his old belt. Three months later, he tore his other ACL.

Finally, in February 2016 -- more than four years after his last title fight -- Cruz challenged TJ Dillashaw for the belt and won a split decision. "I had to show something to myself," Cruz said afterward. "That's what this was."

Tsarukyan's chance to set things right again
Arman Tsarukyan was labeled a snubbed man after it was announced that Justin Gaethje and Paddy Pimblett would headline the first UFC card of 2026 with the No. 1 lightweight contender status at stake. It's hard to remember that sentiment now, considering the year Tsarukyan has had.

In the absence of an obvious UFC fight to take, Tsarukyan has wrestled competitively -- mostly in RAF -- 10 times in 2026. He raised his social media presence exponentially behind videos of lavish cars, extraordinary meals and collaborations with content creator Nina Drama. This is the longest layoff of his UFC career, but his brand has grown more during that time off than from any single fight.

He appears in a good position to get back to work and finally earn the title shot many have said he should have already had. But it won't be an easy fight. Tsarukyan's opponent, Mauricio Ruffy, is a dangerous underdog (+270, according to DraftKings). This fight will restore the order the top of the 155-pound division has lacked in Tsarukyan's absence, regardless of who wins.

Another step for Steveson?

Any MMA prospect would almost certainly switch places with 26-year-old UFC newcomer Gable Steveson. When you're an Olympic gold medal wrestler, and one of the most touted heavyweight prospects in MMA history, certain opportunities are going to come to you that others aren't afforded. It also means Steveson's window for error is small, as he's asked to learn and develop under the sport's brightest lights.

The UFC is managing his opposition. For his second UFC appearance (and fifth pro fight overall), he'll take on Sean Sharaf, a 33-year-old with two knockout losses in his first two UFC fights. Steveson will once again be a heavy, heavy favorite (-2100 by DraftKings), as he was for his promotional debut in July. The heavyweight division is wide open now that Tom Aspinall has vacated his title and the list of top contenders is thin, so Steveson's performance probably means more than the result. If he continues to look the part, his career trajectory could be accelerated at a rate few see.

Coaches' questions and predictions
"Can Pantoja bank enough rounds on the ground, while staying responsible on the feet?"

What a fight this will be. Van shows up in big moments; he's just a proven gamer. If Pantoja stands with Van, he's going to get hurt. Pantoja is good at applying pressure and landing the 1-2 punch (lead left jab, right cross), but he cannot play that game with Van, because of Van's counterboxing. Van's hands are too fast. Van can land four-to-six shots at a time in close distance, and that's something Pantoja really has to watch for. Van is going to have confidence in his ability to get off the ground from his last fight against Taira. I'm going to stay on the fence and say it's a pick 'em. After watching Van's fight with Taira, though, knowing how good Taira is on the ground, it's a little unfair to say Van can't weather the storm on the ground with Pantoja. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Prediction: Too close to call

"How big of a setback is Pantoja's injury at age 36?"
Van is young, fired up and he's got bricks in his hands. We've seen some small weaknesses in his game, which are obviously due to lack of experience. He's getting better all the time. If Pantoja comes back and is anywhere close to where he was when he was holding the belt, I think he gets it back. There are just too many variables on the ground. We saw Van get mounted by Taira. Van is going to go to work on fixing that hole in his game, but Pantoja is so good. The biggest question is how bad of a setback is Pantoja's injury, at this stage of his career? He's not a spring chicken. But if he's the same Pantoja, he gets the win, potentially by submission. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Prediction: Pantoja by decision or submission

"Can Ruffy stop takedowns and keep space?"

Arman has been on such a tear with the wrestling in RAF, showing his ability to wrestle bigger guys and show his power and skill in grappling. When it comes to that, he is very dangerous. Ruffy is finding his groove, and he's very sharp on the feet, but former opponents King Green and Michael Chandler don't pose the same grappling threat that Arman poses. I think Benoît Saint Denis kind of exposed that hole in Ruffy's game. It's not to say Ruffy doesn't have a chance. In space, he is a problem. He can absolutely starch Arman in space. But how does he keep a powerhouse like Arman at distance? -- Saud

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

"Has Ruffy improved his ground defense enough?"
This is a really interesting fight. Arman is going to want to grind out Ruffy. Arman is easily a top-five wrestler/grappler in the UFC. The one thing about Arman -- even though he's stayed busy with the wrestling appearances, he's been out of the UFC for a while, so it'll be interesting to see how he looks. But unless Ruffy catches him and knocks him out, Arman is a good striker, too. Arman can go the distance in a hard fight. My gut leans to Arman. I'm a big fan of Ruffy, but it's just that grappling prowess of Arman. -- Wood

Prediction: Tsarukyan by decision

ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim contributed to this story.

Lewis Hamilton denied he has called for replacements at Ferrari after he admitted his bid for a record eighth world championship is over.

Hamilton threw in the title towel at last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix after he retired from the race in Madrid with a brake problem.

His failure to finish leaves him 101 points behind Kimi Antonelli in the championship standings -- the equivalent of more than four victories -- with just nine scheduled rounds left.

A report in Italy claimed Hamilton has challenged Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur to make changes to the team's trackside staff.

But in a story posted to his Instagram account on Thursday, the 41-year-old wrote: "I've seen some of the stories that have gone out and I want to clear it up on here.

"I've never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced. Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward.

"I always try to empower and lift people to be the best versions of themselves or at least see the best in themselves.

"I may not always achieve that but it's my intention and what I'm here to do. We all work together and that will continue."

- Lando Norris backs 'exciting' 2027 Monaco GP sprint weekend but 'tougher for us drivers'

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time after winning crazy challenge

- F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule

Hamilton sparked hope of challenging Antonelli -- the driver who replaced him at Mercedes -- when he won in Barcelona in June.

However, the British driver has not finished on the podium at the past five rounds and has been openly critical of his team's race tactics.

He also took aim at teammate Charles Leclerc's driving after an opening-lap clash in Monza earlier this month. Hamilton said he led face-to-face talks with the Monegasque to clear the air.

His retirement in Madrid marked his first of the campaign, and when asked to assess his title chances, Hamilton replied: "There's no stopping him [Antonelli] and Mercedes this year. They've done a phenomenal job, and they deserve it [the championship]."

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

stories.headline: Roosters' make call on star forward, Walker progress
stories.summary: Angus Crichton has been cleared to return for the Roosters in their knockout clash with Cronulla, with star halfback Sam Walker not too far behind him.
stories.body:
Test forward Angus Crichton is set to turbo-charge the Sydney Roosters' forward pack as Trent Robinson confirmed the back-rower had received the green light to take on Cronulla.

Crichton, who will move to rugby union whenever the Roosters' season ends, hasn't played since round 15 as a result of a foot injury.

The 30-year-old was a late scratching in last week's qualifying final loss to Penrith.

But Robinson, who provided a glimmer of hope surrounding the fitness of halfback Sam Walker, confirmed 17-time State of Origin star Crichton had been cleared to face the Sharks in Saturday's semi-final at Allianz Stadium.

"(He's) ready to go," Robinson said on Friday.

"I don't think the standard of the game changes when it comes to Angus.

"He'll get on the field but he has played enough of these sort of quality games to get ready to go back in.

"He wasn't ready to go last week, that was the truth of it. He still had some issues last week and he hasn't had them this week, so ready to go."

Young tyro Salesi Foketi would likely make way for Crichton if Robinson chooses to start his experienced edge forward.

"He could start or come off the bench. Gus is ready to go, he'll be in the mix. He's going to hunt," Robinson said.

Victory against the Sharks would send the Roosters into a preliminary final against the Dolphins and Robinson is hopeful Walker will be ready to feature, should his side get past a Cronulla team led by his former protege Craig Fitzgibbon.

Walker underwent ankle surgery three weeks ago but has been back running in a positive sign for Easts' hopes of winning the premiership.

"It's good (Walker had) another good progression this week," Robinson said.

"(He needs to) keep going. There's a little bit less weight on that ankle compared to other guys in our game, so he's progressing well.

"He's a chance (to play next week).

"Most of those guys end up doing running, straight line running, and all of that, whereas he's back into some free movement and into some training, so that's a real positive."

Robinson's side enter Saturday's meeting with Cronulla off a six-day turnaround from the Penrith game and they face the same shortened period of rest if they get past the Sharks to face the Dolphins.

The NRL's finals draw has been complicated by the Warriors making the top four and the flow-on effect of scheduling games at times which suit both Australian and New Zealand broadcasters.

By contrast Newcastle, who face the Warriors on Sunday, will be given a nine-day break between their week-one finals win over Souths.

But Robinson refused to call foul over his side's shortened lead-in to the most important games of the Roosters' season.

"I think we'll do whatever it takes to play finals," Robinson said. "That's as simple as it is.

"I think it's a real fair question around how it's scheduled and why we schedule them in this way, but they're the cards we're dealt and we're ready to play on six days, five days, four days, whatever it takes."

Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to cover the latest fallout from the LA Clippers' punishment after the NBA announced its punishments for the franchise's off-the-court dealings with Kawhi Leonard. They discuss what league history could tell us about what's ahead for the Clippers and how LA got into this situation. Windhorst on the league's reaction to the Clippers' punishment: "I think Steve Balmer had support of his peers in this, even though these was pretty severe accusations.

"I'm not saying everybody again, but I think people wanted to believe him, his peers. I'm not talking about the other GMs. I'm not talking about the agents. ...

"So the word that was said to me by a very influential person was that the other owners, some of the other owners were aghast when they read this report. That was the word that was used to me, aghast. And regardless of what Steve says, the support that he had is no longer there."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action now: "When the Wolves were found guilty, Glen Taylor said words that were not, "I'm guilty." Kevin McHale, who was the vice president of basketball operations, said, 'I didn't even know this existed.' You know, he pled ignorance.

"[Then] They thought about it. They ended up negotiating with the league office and they pled guilty. And two days after basically they raised the white flag in December, David Stern gave him back a pick and a year later he gave him back the second pick. Now he gave them back -- he took away five years of picks [previously] -- he gave them back Year 3 at first and then Year 5. It wasn't like he gave him back immediately. But I think the Clippers should study that."

MacMahon on why Houston extended Thompson now: "I've been telling you for a while just how much the Rockets value Thompson. If there's one untradeable player on the roster, it is him.

"According to their metrics, they think he's one of the top 10 -- and I might be inflating that number -- most valuable players in the league. Now, we can argue and we can debate and you can say that's ridiculous. I'm just telling you the way that they view him. And so for them to get a player they value that much on this deal is great value for them.

"And for Amen Thompson, $208 million fully guaranteed and there's no options either way in the deal, he's set for life. He wants to be in Houston. He's going to be in Houston."

Sept. 3: EMERGENCY POD: NBA announces Clippers' punishments after Kawhi probe
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to react to the hefty punishments handed down to the LA Clippers by the NBA after the investigation into Kawhi Leonard's off-court dealings. They break down what this means for the future of the Clippers, if the punishment makes sense and if this will impact Leonard's pending trade to the Toronto Raptors.

Topics:

1:25: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi probe

7:04 :The Clippers' argument against the NBA in this

10:36: What sticks out about the NBA's findings

16:47: What comes next for the Clippers?

30:21: How will this punishment impact Kawhi?

32:56: Who was most impacted by this punishment?

43:56: Final thoughts on this punishment decision

MacMahon on why the penalty was so large for the Clippers: "The simple fact of the matter is this ain't the first time Steve Balmer's pulled this shady stuff. That did not help his case.

"They gave him a little slap on the wrist for the DeAndre Jordan stuff in 2015. $250,000 fine. It was 'Oh, whoops. We didn't know.' And then, there's the investigation for the Kawhi signing because, guess what? It's not like Uncle Dennis only asked the Clippers for a whole bunch of under-the-table stuff. He was asking everybody for under-the-table stuff. 'Oh, geez. You know, we were asked, but we didn't, you know, didn't give him anything' and and now this. So, in a way they're three-time losers."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action following the ruling: "If they could get an agreement, if they could plead guilty, get an agreement and and say, 'We're not going to challenge any of these penalties.' And they get an agreement that there'll be no further penalties -- basically, they'll say that these five first-round picks are all-encompassing, they cover everything. It's a blanket agreement and [then] they keep their nose clean, and they do the Kawhi trade, they might be able to come out of this without four broken limbs. They may be able to come out of this with less damage."

MacMahon on one of the winners of the investigation: "I do think Adam Silver in a way is a winner of this because straight up, he had been soft on crime as the commissioner since, ironically, he booted the previous Clippers owner, which was completely different circumstances."

stories.body:
Real Madrid and Barcelona could make a future move for USMNT teenager Cavan Sullivan, after his move to Manchester City in 2028, while Arsenal are interested in a move for AFC Bournemouth forward Junior Kroupi in January. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Trending rumors

- Real Madrid and Barcelona could make a future move for USMNT youngster Cavan Sullivan, 16, according to TEAMtalk. The midfielder has impressed since making his breakthrough in MLS as a 14-year-old and has cemented his place in the senior team at Philadelphia Union this season, with six goals and five assists in 23 league appearances. That form has earned him a place in Mauricio Pochettino's most-recent USMNT squad. Sullivan has already agreed to join Manchester City when he turns 18, but the report claims Spain's top two are keeping a close eye on his development and could swoop if he doesn't make the breakthrough into their first XI quickly.

- Arsenal are interested in a move for AFC Bournemouth forward Junior Kroupi in January once he has recovered from injury, says Football.London. Kroupi, 20, scored 13 goals in 35 games last season as the Cherries sealed European football for the first time, but the club would consider offers of over £80 million to let him go. Arsenal already have Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres up front but are looking to strengthen across their forward line after the exits of Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli and Leandro Trossard.

- Bayern Munich are considering a move for Benfica center back Tomás Araújo, according to Tuttomercatoweb. Araújo, 24, is reported to be available for around €40 million but his arrival is reported to be tied to that of Kim Min-Jae and, according to Bild's Christian Falk, Bayern are planning fresh talks with the South Korea international over a new contract. The 29-year-old only has two years left on his deal, which runs until 2028, sparking the discussions about his future. The report claims that it comes as something of a surprise, as Bayern were open to an exit over the summer if the right offer arrived.

- Everton are open to accepting a loan exit for winger Tyler Dibling in the January transfer window, claims Football Insider. The 20-year-old has struggled to assert himself in David Moyes' immediate plans, having failed to make a Premier League appearance so far this season. Development is still the priority for the youngster, whose transfer from Southampton cost £40 million in 2025, and the January window offers an opportunity for Everton to strengthen an already depleted squad before letting him go.

- FC Cincinnati have reached an agreement to sign former Manchester United defender Tyrell Malacia, according to Voetbal International. The left back, who left Old Trafford as a free agent this summer, has reportedly been training with the MLS outfit with the hopes of landing a deal. Now an agreement has been reached, with the report claiming that a deal until mid-2027 has been outlined, with an option to extend by another year. The 27-year-old turned down options in LaLiga and Brazil.

Week 25 is one of the more balanced weeks on the schedule, with one exception: The Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees begin their week-opening series with a Tuesday doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. One of those games makes up their May 23 postponement. The extra game gives both teams a seven-game final week.

All of the other 28 teams play exactly six games -- and 14 of those 28 split those six games evenly between home and the road. This is a "quality over quantity" week when it comes to matchups analysis. Additionally, most teams begin their weeks on Tuesday, as there are only three games scheduled for Monday.

Remember that MLB schedules all games on its final day, Sunday, Sept. 27, to start within a 15 minute window of one another (between 3:05 p.m. and 3:20 p.m. ET). This is by design to try and heighten the drama of real-life playoff races, but it also creates many mad, 3-4 hour dashes to the finish line in fantasy baseball leagues.

stories.summary: Chicago Sky (15-26, 3-14 Eastern Conference) at Atlanta Dream (27-14, 12-5 Eastern Conference)
stories.body:
Chicago Sky (15-26, 3-14 Eastern Conference) at Atlanta Dream (27-14, 12-5 Eastern Conference)

Atlanta; Saturday, 7 p.m. EDT

BOTTOM LINE: Atlanta Dream hosts the Chicago Sky after Angel Reese scored 30 points in the Atlanta Dream's 103-59 victory against the Connecticut Sun.

The Dream's record in Eastern Conference games is 12-5. Atlanta is fourth in the WNBA averaging 91.1 points and is shooting 44.1% from the field.

The Sky are 3-14 in Eastern Conference play. Chicago ranks ninth in the WNBA with 33.1 rebounds per game. Kamilla Cardoso paces the Sky with 8.7.

Atlanta scores 91.1 points per game, 0.9 more points than the 90.2 Chicago allows. Chicago averages 7.3 made 3-pointers per game this season, 1.0 fewer made shot on average than the 8.3 per game Atlanta gives up.

The teams square off for the third time this season. The Dream won the last meeting 93-91 on July 19, with Allisha Gray scoring 29 points in the win.

TOP PERFORMERS: Reese is scoring 16.5 points per game with 12.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists for the Dream. Rhyne Howard is averaging 20.7 points, 4.4 assists and 2.5 steals over the past 10 games.

Cardoso is averaging 14.7 points, 8.7 rebounds and 1.5 blocks for the Sky. Rachel Banham is averaging 1.7 made 3-pointers over the last 10 games.

LAST 10 GAMES: Dream: 8-2, averaging 97.5 points, 38.3 rebounds, 23.4 assists, 8.4 steals and 3.7 blocks per game while shooting 46.1% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 83.0 points per game.

Sky: 3-7, averaging 81.0 points, 34.0 rebounds, 20.6 assists, 6.8 steals and 4.3 blocks per game while shooting 42.4% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 90.9 points.

stories.headline: Alexa Grasso shows off flyweight's elite status in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Former UFC champion puts elite status of women's flyweight division on display in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
It's uncommon for two fighters ranked in the pound-for-pound top 10 to meet in a bout with no championship at stake. But that was the case at Saturday's fourth annual Noche UFC, where Alexa Grasso faced Manon Fiorot.

Grasso is a former women's flyweight champion and Fiorot competed for the belt last year, so their status as MMA elites was well established before they fought. And when Grasso won by unanimous decision, she further solidified her standing in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound rankings.

The top five of the rankings remains intact, and Grasso moves up from 10th to replace Fiorot at No. 6. Fiorot slips two positions to No. 8 in a pound-for-pound hierarchy in which seven of the 10 ranked women compete at flyweight (including Zhang Weili, the former UFC strawweight champion who last fought in an unsuccessful challenge of Valentina Shevchenko in November).

With Shevchenko injured and having vacated her title, there will be much scrambling for the top spot, which will be at stake when No. 5 Natalia Silva fights unranked Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Sept. 16. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Cris Cyborg; 5. Alexa Grasso; 6. Manon Fiorot; 7. Dakota Ditcheva; 8. Natalia Silva; 9. Erin Blanchfield; 10. Tatiana Suarez.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Zhang; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Fiorot; 10. Suarez.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Ditcheva.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

5. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

6. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Alexandre Pantoja

UFC flyweight

Record: 30-6

Last: L (TKO1) vs. Joshua Van, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Sept. 19 vs. Joshua Van

Pantoja became the UFC's unquestioned flyweight king by racking up four title defenses, including two in pay-per-view main events in 2024. He built his winning streak to eight in his UFC 317 win over Kai Kara-France, whom he had already defeated before, like other challengers. But he lost his belt in a gruesome way, injuring his elbow in the opening seconds of a UFC 323 fight with Van. Pantoja gets his rematch with Van at UFC 331.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight interim champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was heralded as the future of the generation when he broke onto the scene, but endured growing pains in losses to Ngannou and Jones. He looks formidable now, and no one will be counting him out if he faces Aspinall in a title unification bout.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight / light heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: TBA

He was on the verge of making history when the opportunity fell apart. Pereira was a UFC champion at middleweight, then light heavyweight, but his unprecedented pursuit of a belt in a third weight class did not go well for the Brazilian, who lost an interim heavyweight title fight to Gane on the White House card. At 39 years old, Pereira does not have much time left to recapture the magic.

stories.headline: I raced against Max Verstappen ... for 10 seconds: Inside the chaos of Max vs 100
stories.summary: ESPN's Nate Saunders might not have lasted long in Max vs 100, but it was still a memorable event. Here, he reflects on his karting experience with Formula 1's Max Verstappen
stories.body:
Few can say they have raced against Max Verstappen -- even if they can only boast that they stayed in front of him for all of 10 seconds.

That was about as long as my challenge lasted in Max vs 100, a wonderfully simple concept on Disney+: put four-time world champion Verstappen at the back of a 101-kart grid at Silverstone and give him 30 laps to pass everybody in front of him. Once he passed you, your race was over.

Starting 89th, I was eliminated before my kart had even reached the front of the grid we were all racing from.

A humbling experience, no doubt: but should an amateur karter going up against one of the greatest drivers of all time have expected any different?

It wasn't just me who had a blink-and-you-missed-it moment against Verstappen. He dispatched an astonishing 64 drivers in that first lap alone and needed only 13 more to catch and overtake everyone else.

Verstappen enjoyed it so much he teased doing it again next year against 200. Seeing how quickly he got things done on Wednesday, you would not bet against him completing that challenge with a handful of laps to spare, either.

Starting as low as I did, there was probably not much chance of any other outcome for me. I already had the excuses ready to explain my lowly grid slot. A spin during one-shot qualifying had turned what was already a middling-to-below-average lap into one only good enough to occupy the 45th row of the grid. Shoot. A blow, I told myself, of getting down to Turn 1 in one piece and an even bigger blow for my chances of staying ahead of Verstappen for even a few corners. Perhaps a better lap and grid position would have given me a better buffer to prevent the inevitable, I reasoned, while Verstappen struggled to get past the slower karts in the field.

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time

- Max Verstappen wins Max vs 100 in style after overtaking 100 go-karters

Turns out the excuses weren't necessary -- an improved grid spot wouldn't have made a shred of difference. As the red lights at the beginning of the start procedure went on one by one, Verstappen had rocked his kart backwards and forwards in a bouncing motion, an old trick he said he learned racing as a seven-year-old. It meant his kart was already rolling well enough to breeze past the karts nearest to him as the lights turned green.

I knew no such tricks, so like the majority of the other amateurs, moved off the line sluggishly as I set about looked for a racing line through the blur of cars down towards Turn 1.

Approximately 10 seconds later, as some space opened up around me as I came off the curve and onto the straight, I glanced to my right.

There he was.

And then, he wasn't.

Verstappen breezed on by as though he was driving a different category of vehicle altogether. As that part of the field got to the first corner, karts were spinning left and right, but he threaded through the chaos like a slalom skier, at one stage simply taking to the grass when the conventional route vanished. My own kart got turned around -- perhaps because I was as much watching the disappearing Verstappen as I was the disappearing bit of unoccupied tarmac in front of me. It is easy to forget when watching trackside or TV the remarkable control of a vehicle professionals had -- Verstappen seemed to be racing on rails, even when he was driving off track to pass karts facing the wrong way.

So that was it. 10 seconds after racing Verstappen had started, my race against Verstappen was over. Brutal stuff indeed.

It all happened so fast that some of the 64 who slowly trundled back into the pit lane after elimination were not even convinced they had seen Verstappen go by. By the time I was out of the kart, he was up to 20th.

"I think the first lap went a bit better than expected, so that helps a lot," Verstappen said later.

Organisers had set a limit of 30 laps but that seemed ludicrously generous as he scythed his way through the field. There had been talk beforehand about trying to defend, working together or even making Verstappen fight for each position. When asked about advice for the 100 karters ahead of the event, Verstappen's long-time rival George Russell had joked that participants should try and go four or five-wide and effectively block the road to stop him advancing. There was, of course, not even the slightest bit of coordination between anyone at the back of the field once the lights went out. Even if we had, Verstappen appeared more than happy to take to the grass on a couple of occasions to get to where he needed to be.

"You just act on instinct, whatever happens when the lights go out, you kind of just see where the gaps are and then you also kind of need to trust the few people around you that they don't do anything crazy," Verstappen said later. "But to be honest, they didn't."

Even if no-one was driving like crazy, the chaos at the start was predictable. Race director and circuit designer David Terrien -- who raced against Max's parents Jos Verstappen and Sophie Kumpen when they were junior karters -- later said he doubted there has ever been a kart race featuring 101 karts. That's not surprising, as there did not seem to be quite enough road to accommodate everyone at the beginning. The grid stretched down the main straight and around a curve. The first lap was almost immediately put under caution -- there were spins, mine included, at Turn 1, while two karts crashed at Turn 3 further up the track so badly that a group of 10 karts got stuck behind.

The circuit worked well when the field had been trimmed down, though, with Verstappen's progress slowing as the amateurs on track were wittled down. He spent six laps in fourth, slowly reeling in the runaway trio at the front.

Verstappen ended up beating one journalist who did, at least, manage to do a better job of representing for the F1 paddock: Dutch reporter Jacky Martens, who finished ahead of YouTuber Zac Alsop and Red Bull's own Lewis Osler to be crowned best of the amateurs. Those last laps were entertaining to watch on the stream, as Verstappen got to utilise the microphones he had fitted to his balaclava to talk to the other competitors around him. "I'm coming for you," he said to a contestant at one stage. Later, he told commentators Alex Jacques and Matt Gallagher: "They need to focus because I'm definitely catching them."

Several of those who remained at least got to properly experience what racing Verstappen is all about. Late in the contest, one of the racers joked to Verstappen -- via a microphone which linked the Dutchman to drivers he approached -- that all he could hear in his head was the famous song about him: "Duh Duh Duh Duh, Max Verstappen, Duh Duh Duh Duh."

Another turned to Verstappen as he approached, laughing and putting his hands together as if begging him not to overtake. He's not the only one to have felt like this with the Dutchman approaching him at alarming speed. McLaren CEO Zak Brown joked last year, as Verstappen started reeling in McLaren pair Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri in the championship, that Verstappen was like the T-Rex in Jurassic Park, seen chasing the car in the mirror with the warning 'Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.' My experience of being passed by Verstappen was so quick I didn't even get the chance to experience the fear.

For Verstappen, it seemed like enormous fun -- he later said he had not driven a proper go-kart since 2016. In a year which has seen Verstappen's love of Formula 1 tested on a massive scale, he later joked he would cherish his winners' trophy as it was his first of the year so far.

Verstappen recently signed a contract to stay in Formula 1 with Red Bull into 2030, ending several years of speculation about moves elsewhere. It's perhaps not surprising he can't imagine a future away from the company which first brought him into Formula 1 as a 17-year-old in 2015. "It's just great that with Red Bull they always come up with some crazy fun things and it suits me as well," he said. "I can really be myself and I think also the way it was organised today, I know that it requires a lot of effort to be able to do something like this."

Whether I'll be there on the grid with him for a future event remains to be seen -- if Wednesday's contest had been an audition to race against a Formula 1 legend again, I dismally failed.

But, given how Verstappen did make almost 100 people look like complete amateurs, there doesn't seem to be too much shame in that.

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

- Borussia Dortmund teenager Karetsas hospitalised after slumping to turf in Champions League

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: 'It's all on': Fitzgibbon relishes Robbo coaching duel
stories.summary: Mates and mentors Craig Fitzgibbon and Trent Robinson have banned contact this week as the Cronulla and Sydney Roosters coaches chase an NRL preliminary final.
stories.body:
No more Mr Nice Guy, Craig Fitzgibbon has shoved friendship aside as he plots to shatter the Sydney Roosters' NRL title hopes for a second successive season.

After a decorated playing career with the Roosters, highlighted by his Clive Churchill-winning display in the Tricolours' 2002 premiership triumph, Fitzgibbon enjoyed a fruitful decade working under Trent Robinson as the club's assistant coach.

But that friendly relationship is on ice this week, with Fitzgibbon, wearing his Cronulla coaching hat, intent on ending the Roosters' season as the Sharks did last year with a 20-10 first-week ambush.

"It was a long time. I've had 10 years working with Trent, so it's definitely a long apprenticeship," Fitzgibbon said ahead of Saturday night's do-or-die battle at Allianz Stadium.

"I had plenty of lessons and am forever grateful for my time there and his mentoring of me to be a coach.

"And he was always supportive and backed me in to take the opportunity when that comes, so I'll be forever grateful for that.

"But this week is about Sharks versus Roosters and, whilst we talk regularly, we're not talking this week."

The latest episode in the pair's coaching rivalry will be the third time in the past four seasons that Cronulla and the Roosters clash in a sudden-death final, with Fitzgibbon and Robinson splitting the first two September showdowns.

The Roosters edged the Sharks 13-12 in 2023 before last year's loss.

Texting is taboo this week, with Fitzgibbon happy to wait until after fulltime to rekindle their great mateship.

"He's fine with that too," Fitzgibbon said.

"He's just as competitive as I am so, no, we'll shut it down this week. We've bumped into each other in plenty of semis now, so it's a contest and it's a game.

"A lot of work goes into a whole season, starting all the way back in the November before, so the ups and downs of the season.

"But you get to this end and it's all on."

Both sides fumbled and bumbled their way into this year's finals, the Sharks losing four of their last five regular-season games with star five-eighth Braydon Trindall sidelined with a dislocated shoulder.

After briefly sharing premiership favouritism after taking down Penrith in round 24, the Roosters also lost playmaker Sam Walker to an ankle injury during a run of four straight defeats.

While below the form that led the Sharks to nine wins from 10 starts before their slump, Fitzgibbon saw enough in last Saturday's 26-16 victory over North Queensland to be heartened.

"We played more like Sharks," he said.

"A bit more cohesion back in. Obviously there were some changes in and out and then we set on the line-up and got back to playing like we know we can.

"It was probably really physical early and we had to stay in the fight there for a bit and then managed to come out the other side and dealt with a couple of disallowed tries and dealt with a little bit of adversity to be able to not get flustered and stick to the plan."

Saturday night's victors will advance to a preliminary final against the Dolphins at Suncorp Stadium next Friday night.
